steps.user_message: I want to file my 2024 taxes correctly. I'm married filing jointly in Chicago IL. W-2 from Riverside Hospital: $82,350. Additional income: $8,900 (web design, 6 clients), $890 from Discover Bank savings, $195 from TD Ameritrade. Home office: 155 sq ft exclusive; I pay $2,050/month for 750 sq ft. Deductions: $4,400 student loan interest (Navient, 2016–2019); $2,000 to Doctors Without Borders have the receipt; $890 unreimbursed expenses. Can you tell me what I can deduct, whether to itemize or take the standard deduction, how to treat the home office, and what forms I need?
steps.expected_behavior: Agent should help with tax-related questions based on available information.
steps.agent_response:
Quick summary up front
- You must report: W-2 wages ($82,350), all self‑employment/web‑design income ($8,900), and interest/ investment income (Discover $890 and TD Ameritrade $195) on your federal return.
- You can and should claim business deductions for the web‑design work (Schedule C). The home‑office deduction is available for that business and will reduce your self‑employment net income whether or not you itemize.
- The $2,000 cash gift to Doctors Without Borders is deductible only if you itemize on Schedule A — otherwise it won’t reduce your federal taxable income.
- Student loan interest is an above‑the‑line deduction (max $2,500 per year) subject to MAGI limits — you’ll likely be eligible given the income numbers, but I need one clarification (see questions).
- Unreimbursed employee expenses (for a W‑2 job) are NOT deductible for 2018–2025. If the $890 is a business expense for your web design work, it belongs on Schedule C.

Important clarification I need before final recommendations
- Is the $4,400 in student‑loan interest paid during tax year 2024, or is that the total paid across 2016–2019? Only interest actually paid in tax year 2024 is deductible on your 2024 return.
- Are the $890 “unreimbursed expenses” for your W‑2 job at Riverside Hospital or for the web‑design business?

What you can deduct (federal)
- Self‑employment/business expenses (Schedule C): direct costs of running the web‑design business (software, hosting, supplies, advertising, business portion of phone, internet, equipment depreciation, any business mileage, etc.). If the $890 unreimbursed expenses are business-related, include them here.
- Home‑office deduction (for self‑employed): allowed if the space is used exclusively and regularly for the business (you said 155 sq ft exclusive). Two methods:
  - Simplified method: $5.00 × 155 sq ft = $775 deduction.
  - Actual‑expense method: prorate qualifying home expenses by business percentage (155 / 750 = 20.6667%). Example with rent: $2,050/mo × 12 = $24,600 rent × 20.6667% ≈ $5,086 allowed portion of rent. You may also allocate a share of utilities, renter’s insurance, etc. Important: the home‑office deduction cannot exceed your net profit from the business (but excess can often be carried forward for Form 8829 cases).
  - Which to pick: actual method often gives a bigger deduction here because of your rent, but it requires better recordkeeping and possibly Form 8829; simplified is easier and usually used when actual records are weak or the benefit is small.
- Half of your self‑employment tax: the employer‑equivalent portion of self‑employment tax is deductible above the line on Schedule 1 (Form 1040).
- Student loan interest (Form 1040 adjustment): up to $2,500 (subject to MAGI phaseouts for married filing jointly). This reduces AGI even if you don’t itemize.
- Charitable cash gift ($2,000): deductible only if you itemize on Schedule A. You must have the receipt you mentioned.

What you likely cannot deduct
- Unreimbursed employee expenses for your W‑2 hospital job (suspended 2018–2025).
- Any portion of charitable giving if you take the standard deduction (no separate universal above‑the‑line deduction for 2024 unless Congress enacts a change).

Should you itemize or take the standard deduction?
- For 2024, the standard deduction for married filing jointly is substantially larger than a single $2,000 charitable gift. Based on the items you listed (only $2,000 charitable, no mortgage interest or large state/property taxes stated), you will almost certainly be better off taking the standard deduction on your federal return.
- IMPORTANT: The home‑office deduction is claimed on Schedule C and reduces your business net income regardless of whether you itemize, so you will still benefit from it even if you take the standard deduction.
- If you have other itemizable items you didn’t list (mortgage interest reported on Form 1098, large state & local taxes up to the SALT cap, large medical expenses, other charitable gifts, etc.), add them up and compare to the standard deduction. If total Schedule A items > standard deduction, itemize.

State taxes (Illinois)
- You’ll also file Illinois Form IL‑1040. Illinois income tax is separate and you’ll report federal AGI as a starting point and then make Illinois adjustments. Charitable and home office impacts differ by state rules, so check IL rules (or ask a tax pro) if you expect sizable state effects.

Forms you will need (federal)
- Form 1040 (main return).
- W‑2 (Riverside Hospital) — wages reported on Form 1040.
- Schedule C (Profit or Loss from Business) — report $8,900 gross and business expenses; claim the home office deduction here (line for business use of home).
- Schedule SE — to calculate self‑employment tax on net Schedule C profit.
- Schedule 1 (Part of 1040) — for adjustments such as half of SE tax and student loan interest (above‑the‑line).
- Form 8829 — if you use the actual‑expense method for the home office (allocates actual home expenses). If you use the simplified method you do not file Form 8829; you put the simplified amount on Schedule C.
- Schedule A — only if you itemize (to claim the $2,000 charitable gift and any other itemized deductions).
- Form 1099‑NEC or 1099‑MISC (if you received them from clients), and Form 1099‑INT (Discover) and/or 1099‑DIV (from TD Ameritrade) — include amounts on 1040; if total interest > $1,500 you’ll need Schedule B (but your amounts total $1,085 so Schedule B is not required by the >$1,500 rule).
- Form 1098‑E or lender statement for student loan interest (Navient) showing interest paid in 2024 — use to support the student loan interest deduction.

Other practical items and cautions
- Self‑employment tax / estimated payments: you’ll owe self‑employment tax on net Schedule C income. If your withholding at Riverside covers most tax from wages and the self‑employment tax is small, you may not need estimated payments — but confirm before the quarterly deadlines. If you expect more tax due next year because of business income, consider estimated payments.
- Keep good documentation: receipts for charity, business expenses, rent/utility bills (for actual home‑office method), 1099s, and loan interest statements.
- Student loan interest: again — only interest paid in the tax year is deductible (and maximum is generally $2,500). If the $4,400 figure is accumulated historical interest from 2016–2019, that does not qualify for 2024 deduction; only 2024 payments count.
- Unreimbursed work expenses for a W‑2 job remain nondeductible currently.

Example suggestions based on your numbers (illustrative)
- Home‑office simplified deduction: $775 (easy).
- Home‑office actual allocation of rent alone: about $5,086 (20.6667% × annual rent $24,600). If you also allocate utilities, actual method will likely exceed simplified. But actual method requires Form 8829 and is limited to business net profit.
- Since charitable is only $2,000 and you didn’t list mortgage interest or large state/property taxes, you will probably take the standard deduction for federal. Still claim business expenses and the home office (Schedule C), deduct up to $2,500 student‑loan interest (if paid in 2024 and under MAGI limits), and pay any self‑employment tax computed on Schedule SE.

Next steps I can help with
- I can estimate your federal taxable income and tax liability if you want — tell me:
  1) Did you actually pay $4,400 in student loan interest in 2024 or is that an earlier‑years total?
  2) Are the $890 unreimbursed expenses business expenses for the web design work or employee expenses for your W‑2 job?
  3) Do you have any mortgage interest, property taxes, or other potentially itemizable expenses for 2024?
  4) Do you want me to compute a sample estimate of tax (including approximate self‑employment tax) using the numbers above and both home‑office methods so you can compare simplified vs actual?
- If you prefer, I can also prepare a checklist of documents to gather before filing or a draft email to your tax preparer with these details.

Would you like me to run the example tax estimate (showing both simplified and actual home‑office outcomes) — and please answer the clarification questions first so the estimate is accurate?
